label: Chapter 7: Rebuilding and Founding Europe, 1945 to 1980

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: When the war ended, Luxembourg drew a conclusion that would shape the rest of its history.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A small country cannot protect itself by standing alone.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Neutrality had been tried and had failed twice.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So the Grand Duchy threw itself into international cooperation with an enthusiasm few larger countries could match.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It started before the war even ended.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In September 1944, with the exiled governments of Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg still in London, they signed an agreement to create a customs union.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The name was a combination of their initials: Benelux.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Fourteen years later, they turned it into a full economic union.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then a flurry of firsts.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1945, Luxembourg became a founding member of the United Nations.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1948, it rewrote its constitution to remove the clause that made it perpetually neutral.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1949, it was one of the twelve founding members of NATO.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For a country with a tiny army, that was a bold declaration.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Luxembourg was firmly part of the Western camp.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the most important step had Luxembourg connections of a different kind.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Robert Schuman was born in 1886 in Clausen, a neighborhood of Luxembourg City, to a Luxembourg mother and a father from the French region of Lorraine.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He grew up speaking German, French and Luxembourgish, studied in Germany, and eventually became a French politician.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After the Second World War he served as France's foreign minister.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And on the ninth of May, 1950...

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Schuman proposed that France and Germany, who had fought three wars in less than a century, should place their coal and steel production under a single common authority, open to other European countries.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: If the raw materials of war were jointly controlled, a new war between the two would become unthinkable.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That is the Schuman Declaration, and May ninth is celebrated today as Europe Day.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the result was...

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The European Coal and Steel Community, set up in 1951 by six countries: France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Luxembourg was a natural participant.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It made more steel per head than almost anyone, ARBED was one of the giants of the sector, and its leaders had learned that tying themselves to bigger neighbors in shared institutions was the best way to stay free.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And there was another key figure.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Joseph Bech, Luxembourg's foreign minister for more than thirty years, from 1926 to 1958.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1955, at a conference in the Sicilian town of Messina, he helped push forward a plan for a wider common market.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That led to the Treaties of Rome in 1957, which created the European Economic Community, the direct ancestor of today's European Union.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Small government, skilled diplomats.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They made themselves useful as mediators between France and Germany.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Luxembourg was rewarded. The High Authority of the Coal and Steel Community was based there from 1952.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So was the Court of Justice, which still sits in Luxembourg today.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1968, the European Investment Bank set up its headquarters there, and in 1977 the European Court of Auditors followed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Parts of the European Parliament's administration are there too, along with Eurostat, the EU's statistics office.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: In a continent of far larger capitals...

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The little city on the Alzette had quietly become one of the capitals of Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it lent its name to a famous diplomatic fix.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1965, France's president Charles de Gaulle was furious about plans to give the European institutions more power, and he boycotted meetings for months.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That was the empty chair crisis.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was settled in January 1966 at a meeting in Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The deal, known as the Luxembourg Compromise, effectively let a country block a decision if its vital national interests were at stake.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For decades afterwards it shaped how Europe made decisions.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Back home, the country was rebuilding.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The north, devastated by the Battle of the Bulge, was rebuilt town by town.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Steel boomed in the postwar decades, as Europe needed girders, rails and machinery.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Wages rose, new housing went up, and the standard of living climbed steadily.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the throne changed hands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Grand Duchess Charlotte, who had reigned for forty-five years and become the symbol of the country's survival, abdicated on the twelfth of November, 1964, in favor of her son Jean.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Jean, who had fought alongside the Allies, was forty-three, and he would reign for thirty-six years.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And a quieter change.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The steel mills needed workers, and Luxembourg's own population was too small to supply them.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Starting in the nineteen-sixties, thousands of people arrived from Portugal, escaping poverty and a dictatorship at home.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They worked in construction, in the mills, in hotels and restaurants.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They became the largest foreign community in the country, and today people of Portuguese origin make up about one in seven residents.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So Luxembourg was multicultural long before that was fashionable.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And then there was a financial first.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1963, an Italian motorway company raised money through a new kind of bond, sold outside its home country and denominated in a foreign currency.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was the first so-called Eurobond, and it was listed on the Luxembourg stock exchange.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Why Luxembourg?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Simple. It was friendly, flexible, discreet, and lightly regulated.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Over the next decade, banks from Germany, the United States and elsewhere arrived to set up shop.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was the seed of a new economy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And someone saw where it was going.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Pierre Werner, prime minister and finance minister for much of the sixties and seventies.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1970, European leaders asked a committee chaired by Werner to design a path toward a single European currency.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Werner Report mapped out a step-by-step plan for monetary union by 1980.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was shelved after the monetary chaos of the early seventies and the oil crisis, but its ideas came back twenty years later.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The euro, launched in 1999, owes something to the plan sketched by a Luxembourg politician in 1970.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then the oil crisis hit.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The crisis of 1973 and the global steel crisis that followed hit Luxembourg hard.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Steel demand collapsed and the southern mills were in danger.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1977, rather than let mass unemployment tear society apart, the government brought unions and employers together in a standing body called the Tripartite.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They negotiated early retirements, retraining and state support, and avoided the bitter strikes and layoffs that wrecked other industrial regions.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: This approach of consensus became known as the Luxembourg model.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Now a lighter note.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In these same years, Luxembourg quietly became a pop music superpower.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Radio Luxembourg, broadcasting in English by night on medium wave, was one of the few ways British teenagers could hear the latest records.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Many remember listening under the blankets with a transistor radio.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Eurovision.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Luxembourg won five times: in 1961, 1965, 1972, 1973, and 1983.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One winner was the French singer France Gall, who won in 1965 with a song written by Serge Gainsbourg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A country of a few hundred thousand people won more often than many far larger ones, helped by its commercial radio and its talent for hiring great singers from abroad.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Luxembourg that had been invaded and half-destroyed was a comfortable, cosmopolitan little state with a seat at Europe's table.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the steel that had made it rich was in decline.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the answer to what would replace it...

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Was money.
